reigns.tagline: Twice a king of Poland, and twice chased out
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rival king, chosen by Charles XII
reigns.previously: Augustus the Strong dies. But rewind to 1704 and his Swedish rival.
paragraphs: Stanisław Leszczyński was a cultured, good-natured noble of 26 when Charles XII of Sweden chose him to replace Augustus. A small assembly near Warsaw, guarded by Swedish troops, elected him in July 1704, and he was crowned the next year. He stayed king exactly as long as the Swedish army stood behind him. When Peter the Great destroyed that army at Poltava in 1709, Stanisław had to run.

He ended up in exile in Alsace, short of money and nearly forgotten. Then came a stroke of luck: in 1725 his daughter Marie married the young Louis XV and became Queen of France. When Augustus died in 1733, French money made Stanisław a candidate again. He crossed Germany in secret, reached Warsaw and was elected in September 1733.

Russia and Austria would not have it. A Russian army chased him to Gdańsk and besieged the city in 1734. Stanisław got out before it fell. In the peace deal he gave up Poland for the Duchy of Lorraine, his for life. He spent 30 happy years there, building and writing, and died in 1766 at 88 after his dressing gown caught fire.

claims.text: Stanisław escaped besieged Gdańsk disguised as a peasant.
claims.note: He certainly slipped out before the city surrendered. The colourful disguise comes from his own and his friends' later retellings.

claims.text: He died after his dressing gown caught fire by the hearth.
claims.note: Reported at Lunéville at the time. He lingered for some days with his burns before he died.

claims.text: His daughter Marie became Queen of France.
claims.note: She married Louis XV in 1725 and was queen for over 40 years.

reigns.hook: Stanisław has fled Gdańsk. The Russians already have their own man on the throne: Augustus the Strong's son, who would much rather be in Dresden.

reigns.tagline: The absentee king of fine paintings and broken parliaments
reigns.previously: Stanisław flees Gdańsk. Russia's candidate, Augustus III, takes over.
paragraphs: Augustus III got Poland the way his father got it back: with foreign help. A small group of nobles elected him on 5 October 1733 while a Russian army stood by, and he was crowned in Kraków in January 1734. The Russians then besieged Gdańsk and drove out his rival. This was the War of the Polish Succession, and it was Poland's neighbours who settled it.

Augustus much preferred Dresden. He loved hunting, opera and pictures, and he bought Raphael's Sistine Madonna for his gallery there. The hard work he left to his minister, Count Heinrich von Brühl, famous for his lavish wardrobe. In Poland the great magnate families ran their own politics, and almost every Sejm of the reign broke up without passing a single law.

Still, there were 30 years of peace inside Poland, and the nobles remembered them fondly. When Prussia overran Saxony in 1756, Augustus spent most of the Seven Years' War in Warsaw. He went home in 1763 and died in Dresden on 5 October, 30 years to the day after his election.

claims.text: Nobles summed up the age: 'Under the Saxon king, eat, drink and loosen your belt.'
claims.note: A genuine old Polish saying. It captures how the era was remembered, not hard history.

claims.text: Only one Sejm in his 30 years managed to finish its work.
claims.note: The usual count says only the 1736 'pacification' Sejm passed laws; historians differ on how to count the rest.

reigns.hook: Augustus III is dead. Catherine the Great of Russia already knows who the next King of Poland will be: a charming young Pole who was once her lover.

reigns.tagline: The last king, who watched his country vanish
reigns.previously: Augustus III dies in Dresden. Catherine the Great picks the next king.
paragraphs: Stanisław Poniatowski was clever, charming and well read. As a young diplomat in St Petersburg he had an affair with the Grand Duchess Catherine. Once she was Empress, she made him King of Poland, with Russian troops close to the election field in 1764. She expected a puppet. He wanted to reform the country, which made Russia angry and many Polish nobles suspicious.

Conservative nobles formed the Confederation of Bar in 1768 and fought both Russia and the king. In 1771 some of them kidnapped him in Warsaw, but he talked one captor round and got away. In 1772 Russia, Prussia and Austria took almost a third of the country in the First Partition. Stanisław kept going. He set up the Commission of National Education, hosted Thursday dinners for writers and filled Warsaw with art.

The Great Sejm passed the Constitution of 3 May 1791, one of the first modern written constitutions anywhere. Magnates of the Targowica Confederation called in Russia, and the king gave way. The Second Partition followed in 1793. Kościuszko's uprising of 1794 was crushed, and in 1795 the rest of Poland was shared out. On 25 November Stanisław abdicated. He died in St Petersburg in 1798.

claims.text: Catherine the Great made her former lover King of Poland.
claims.note: Stanisław's own memoirs and Catherine's writings both describe the affair, and her backing for him in 1764 is well documented.

claims.text: Kidnapped by Bar confederates, he talked one of his captors into letting him go.
claims.note: Well documented; the kidnappers were later put on trial in Warsaw.

claims.text: The 3 May Constitution was Europe's first modern written constitution.
claims.note: Widely said in Poland. It did come months before France's, though Corsica's constitution of 1755 is sometimes counted as earlier.

reigns.hook: There is no king and no Poland. Russia, Prussia and Austria have split the land three ways. But Polish soldiers are marching with Napoleon, and a quiet Saxon, Frederick Augustus, will be their duke.

reigns.tagline: Napoleon's Polish duchy and its Saxon duke
reigns.cameToPower: Made Duke of Warsaw by Napoleon
reigns.previously: Stanisław August abdicates. Poland disappears from the map.
paragraphs: After 1795 there was no Poland on the map. Poles kept fighting anyway. In 1797 General Jan Henryk Dąbrowski raised Polish legions in Italy to fight for Napoleon, and Józef Wybicki wrote them a marching song: "Poland has not yet perished, so long as we live." It is now the national anthem. Napoleon smashed Prussia in 1806, and at Tilsit in July 1807 he cut a small Polish state out of Prussia's share: the Duchy of Warsaw.

Its duke was a mild, devout Saxon. Frederick Augustus had been Elector of Saxony since he was 12, and Napoleon had just made him a king. He was Augustus III's grandson, and the 3 May Constitution of 1791 had named him heir to the Polish throne. The duchy got a constitution and the Napoleonic Code. Serfdom was abolished, though the peasants got their freedom without any land. The duke ran things mostly from Dresden.

The real star was Prince Józef Poniatowski, the last king's nephew, who led the army. In 1809 he fought off an Austrian invasion and took Kraków, nearly doubling the duchy. In 1812 close to 100,000 Poles marched on Moscow with Napoleon, and few came back. At Leipzig in October 1813 Poniatowski drowned covering the retreat, and Frederick Augustus, loyal to Napoleon to the end, was taken prisoner by the Allies.

claims.text: The 3 May 1791 constitution named Frederick Augustus the next King of Poland.
claims.note: It made the Elector of Saxony Stanisław August's successor, with the crown hereditary in his line. He held back from accepting while Russia was against it.

claims.text: 'Dąbrowski's Mazurka' was first sung by the Polish legions in Italy in 1797.
claims.note: Wybicki wrote it at Reggio Emilia in July 1797. It became the official national anthem in 1927.

claims.text: Poniatowski cried that God had given him the honour of the Poles and he would give it back only to God, then rode into the river.
claims.note: Witnesses agree he was wounded and drowned in the Elster on 19 October 1813. The famous last words appear only in later accounts.

reigns.hook: Napoleon is finished and his Polish duchy is up for grabs. At the Congress of Vienna, Tsar Alexander I wants it all, and he is happy to call himself King of Poland to get it.

reigns.title: The Partitions
reigns.tagline: A tsar for a king, and a century of risings
reigns.previously: Napoleon falls, and Vienna hands most of the duchy to the tsar.
paragraphs: The Congress of Vienna split the duchy up again. Prussia took Poznań, Kraków became a tiny free city, and the biggest piece became a Kingdom of Poland with the Russian tsar as its king. Alexander I gave it a liberal constitution, its own army and a parliament. His brother Constantine ran that army from Warsaw like a bully. In November 1830 young officers rose up. In January 1831 the Sejm declared Nicholas I dethroned, and Russia crushed the rising that year.

Thousands went west in the Great Emigration, among them Chopin and the poet Mickiewicz, with Prince Adam Czartoryski as their leader in Paris. Russia scrapped the constitution and the army. In January 1863 Poles rose again, in a hopeless guerrilla war that lasted over a year. Its last leader, Romuald Traugutt, was hanged at the Warsaw Citadel in August 1864. Then came Russification: Russian in schools and offices, and officials started calling the place the "Vistula Land".

Prussia, later Germany, leaned on its Poles too, while Austria gave Galicia home rule and let Kraków become a Polish cultural capital. Maria Skłodowska, born in Warsaw, studied in secret before winning two Nobel Prizes in France. In 1914 the three empires went to war with each other. Germany took Warsaw in 1915 and later set up a puppet Regency Council. By November 1918 all three empires had collapsed, and on 11 November Poland was free.

claims.text: In January 1831 the Polish Sejm dethroned the tsar as King of Poland.
claims.note: The vote of 25 January 1831 turned the November Uprising into an open war with Russia.

claims.text: Romuald Traugutt, the January Uprising's last leader, was hanged in Warsaw.
claims.note: Arrested in April 1864, he was executed with four comrades below the Warsaw Citadel on 5 August 1864.

claims.text: Maria Skłodowska studied at Warsaw's secret 'Flying University'.
claims.note: She described it herself: an underground college that moved from flat to flat to dodge the tsar's police.

reigns.hook: Poland is back, but its borders are unsettled and enemies circle on every side. Power falls to a former train robber who spent years in Russian and German hands: Józef Piłsudski.

reigns.tagline: The train robber who brought Poland back to life
reigns.cameToPower: Handed power by the Regency Council
reigns.previously: After 123 years of partition, Poland is back on the map.
paragraphs: No more kings now. From here we follow whoever really held power, and in 1918 that was Józef Piłsudski. Born near Vilnius in 1867, he did five years in Siberia as a young man, became a socialist revolutionary, and in 1908 helped rob a Russian mail train at Bezdany for party funds. In the First World War he raised Polish Legions, then fell out with the Germans and landed in a Magdeburg prison. Freed in November 1918, he came home to Warsaw a hero.

As Chief of State he fought on every border. In 1920 the Red Army reached the gates of Warsaw, and in August Piłsudski's counter-attack smashed it, the "Miracle on the Vistula". In 1922 he handed over to an elected president, Gabriel Narutowicz, who was shot dead by a nationalist fanatic within days. Fed up with squabbling politicians, Piłsudski marched on Warsaw in May 1926 and seized power in a three-day coup.

He refused the presidency. He didn't need it. As "the Marshal" and minister of war he ran the country from behind the scenes, and jailed opposition leaders when they got in his way. He died on 12 May 1935. His body went to Wawel with the kings; his heart went to Vilnius, buried with his mother.

claims.text: Piłsudski took part in the armed robbery of a Russian mail train at Bezdany in 1908.
claims.note: He led the raid himself; the woman who became his second wife, Aleksandra Szczerbińska, was among the plotters. The money went to his fighting organisation.

claims.text: The 1920 victory was a miracle, or the work of French advisers rather than Piłsudski.
claims.note: The phrase was spread by his political enemies to deny him credit. Historians give the plan to Piłsudski and his chief of staff Tadeusz Rozwadowski; French general Weygand himself said the victory was Polish.

claims.text: His heart is buried in Vilnius in his mother's grave.
claims.note: It was placed in the Rasos cemetery in 1936 under a black granite slab, as he had asked.

reigns.hook: The Marshal is dead and nobody can fill his boots. His state passes to two of his men, President Mościcki and General Rydz-Śmigły, with Hitler to the west and Stalin to the east.

reigns.title: The President and the Marshal
reigns.tagline: Piłsudski's heirs, a new constitution and no way out
reigns.previously: Piłsudski dies. His heart goes to Vilnius, his body to Wawel.
paragraphs: Weeks before he died, Piłsudski's camp pushed through a constitution that put a strong president on top. The president was Ignacy Mościcki, a chemistry professor who had made his name with a new way of producing nitric acid, picked by Piłsudski for the job in 1926. The army went to General Edward Rydz-Śmigły, a trained painter turned Legion commander. He was made a Marshal in 1936, and was soon officially second only to the president.

The two men kept an uneasy balance, while Colonel Józef Beck ran foreign policy. The regime, called Sanation from the Latin for healing, squeezed the opposition, and nationalist pressure on Jews grew, with separate benches for Jewish students at some universities. Beck tried to balance between Berlin and Moscow and tie Poland to neither. When Germany carved up Czechoslovakia in 1938, Poland sent an ultimatum and grabbed the Zaolzie district too.

Then Hitler turned on Poland, demanding Danzig and a road across Polish land. Britain promised to defend Poland on 31 March 1939. On 5 May Beck told the Sejm no: peace was precious, but honour had no price. In August, Hitler and Stalin signed a pact with a secret clause splitting Poland between them.

claims.text: Beck refused Hitler's demands in a speech saying honour was the one thing without price.
claims.note: He spoke to the Sejm on 5 May 1939. The speech was hugely popular in Poland and is still quoted.

claims.text: Poland took part in the break-up of Czechoslovakia.
claims.note: After the Munich deal, Warsaw issued an ultimatum on 30 September 1938 and Polish troops entered Zaolzie days later.

claims.text: Piłsudski picked Rydz-Śmigły as his successor.
claims.note: He had marked Rydz-Śmigły out as the next head of the army, but he named no political heir, which is why power ended up shared.

reigns.title: War and Occupation
reigns.tagline: Invaded from both sides, and the Holocaust on Polish soil
reigns.previously: Beck says no to Hitler. Hitler and Stalin secretly carve it up.
paragraphs: Germany invaded on 1 September 1939. The small garrison at Westerplatte held out for a week. On 17 September the Soviet Union invaded from the east, as agreed with Hitler. Warsaw surrendered on 28 September. A government-in-exile formed, first in France, then in London. Both occupiers set out to destroy Poland as a nation. The Soviets deported hundreds of thousands, and in 1940 their secret police shot about 22,000 Polish officers and others at Katyn and other sites.

Germany ran a regime of mass terror: executions, expulsions, forced labour. It also carried out the Holocaust. About three million Polish Jews were murdered, most of them in death camps that Germany built and ran in occupied Poland, among them Auschwitz-Birkenau and Treblinka. In April 1943 the fighters of the Warsaw Ghetto rose up against the Germans. The Polish underground army grew into one of the largest in occupied Europe.

In July 1943 the exile leader, General Sikorski, was killed in a plane crash at Gibraltar. Polish troops took Monte Cassino in May 1944. On 1 August 1944 the Home Army rose in Warsaw; after 63 days it surrendered, at least 150,000 civilians were dead, and Germany then razed the city. The Red Army stood across the Vistula. At Yalta in February 1945, the Allies agreed to move Poland's borders west. Close to six million Polish citizens died in the war.

claims.text: The Soviet Union carried out the Katyn massacre and blamed it on Germany for nearly 50 years.
claims.note: The NKVD shot the prisoners in April and May 1940. Moscow admitted it only in April 1990, and released the key documents in 1992.

claims.text: Auschwitz, Treblinka and the other death camps were German camps.
claims.note: They were set up and run by Nazi Germany in occupied Poland. Calling them "Polish camps" is simply wrong.

claims.text: Stalin halted the Red Army so the Germans would crush the Warsaw Uprising.
claims.note: His offensive had stalled after a long advance, but he also refused for weeks to let Allied supply planes land on Soviet-held airfields. Historians still argue over how far it was a choice.

reigns.hook: Germany surrenders on 8 May 1945. Poland is on the winning side, but the Red Army stays, and Stalin's chosen men are already in charge in Warsaw.

reigns.tagline: Moscow's man and Poland's Stalinist years
reigns.previously: The war ends. Poland is shifted west, with the Red Army still there.
paragraphs: Bolesław Bierut was a self-taught working man from Lublin who became a communist, spent years in the Soviet Union and sat in a Polish jail in the 1930s. From the start of 1944 he chaired the communists' National Council, and when the war ended he headed the new state. A few exiles came home to join the government, but the communists held the police and the guns.

The 1946 referendum and the 1947 election were both rigged. The parliament made Bierut president, and the opposition leader Mikołajczyk fled abroad. In 1948 Bierut pushed aside his rival Gomułka, later jailing him, and led the new ruling party. Stalinism followed: show trials, torture, collective farms. Witold Pilecki, who had let himself be sent to Auschwitz to report on it, was executed in 1948. The Primate, Cardinal Wyszyński, was locked up in 1953.

Stalin's "gift", the giant Palace of Culture, rose over Warsaw. In February 1956 Bierut went to Moscow for the Soviet party congress, where Khrushchev denounced Stalin in a secret speech. Bierut fell ill there and never came home alive. He died on 12 March 1956.

claims.text: The 1946 referendum results were faked.
claims.note: Archive research has shown the published figures were made up; most voters had actually rejected at least one of the communists' questions.

claims.text: Bierut was poisoned in Moscow.
claims.note: There is no evidence. The rumour, and the Polish joke that he "went in a fur coat and came back in a box", grew from the timing, days after the Secret Speech.

claims.text: Witold Pilecki volunteered to be sent to Auschwitz.
claims.note: He got himself caught in a Warsaw round-up in 1940, organised resistance in the camp, escaped in 1943 and wrote detailed reports.

reigns.hook: Bierut's death leaves the party leaderless just as Khrushchev's attack on Stalin starts to leak. Khrushchev himself flies to Warsaw for the funeral, and stays to see who comes next.

reigns.tagline: The stopgap boss who handed over the keys
reigns.previously: Bierut dies in Moscow, days after Khrushchev denounces Stalin.
paragraphs: Khrushchev came to Warsaw for Bierut's funeral and stayed to watch the party pick a new leader. On 20 March 1956 the Central Committee chose Edward Ochab, a Kraków-born communist who had done time in pre-war Polish jails and come home in 1944 with the Polish army raised in the USSR. He looked a safe pair of hands.

But Khrushchev's secret speech against Stalin spread fast in Poland, and Ochab let the thaw run. A big amnesty that spring freed thousands of prisoners. Then, on 28 June, workers at Poznań's huge engineering works marched into town demanding bread and freedom. Crowds besieged the secret police building, and the army was sent in with tanks. Dozens were killed. The regime blamed foreign agents, but everyone knew better.

Over the summer the party split. Hardliners wanted a crackdown; reformers wanted Gomułka, the man Bierut had jailed. Ochab came down on the reformers' side. In October, with Soviet troops on the move, he stepped aside and let Gomułka take the top job. He stayed in the leadership and later served as head of state, until he quit in 1968.

claims.text: Khrushchev sat in on the meeting that chose Ochab.
claims.note: He had come for Bierut's funeral and attended the Central Committee plenum of 20 March 1956.

claims.text: Ochab gave up the party leadership of his own accord to make way for Gomułka.
claims.note: He backed Gomułka's return at the October plenum and stayed on in the leadership, a rare peaceful handover in the Soviet bloc.

claims.text: Ochab quit as head of state in 1968 rather than back the anti-Jewish campaign.
claims.note: He resigned in April 1968, at the height of the campaign. Most historians read it as a protest, but he said little in public.

reigns.hook: Moscow is alarmed. On 19 October Khrushchev flies into Warsaw uninvited, with Soviet tanks rolling towards the capital, to face the man the Poles now want.

reigns.tagline: The reformer who faced down Khrushchev, then went sour
reigns.previously: Ochab steps aside for the man Bierut once jailed.
paragraphs: Edward Ochab led the party for a few months after Bierut. In June 1956 the workers of Poznań rose up, and the army crushed them, killing dozens. The party needed someone people might trust. It found Władysław Gomułka, a former fitter with a limp from a police bullet, who had led the wartime communist underground and spent over three years in jail under Bierut.

On 19 October Khrushchev flew into Warsaw uninvited while Soviet tanks moved. Gomułka stood his ground, and two days later he was party leader. Collective farms were broken up, the Cardinal was freed, and huge crowds cheered. The thaw didn't last. In 1968 he crushed student protests and led a campaign against "Zionists" that drove most of Poland's remaining Jews out of the country. Polish troops joined the invasion of Czechoslovakia.

In December 1970 he signed a treaty with West Germany accepting Poland's new western border. Days later his government raised food prices just before Christmas. The shipyards of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Szczecin went on strike, and troops and police opened fire. Officially 41 people were killed. Gomułka was out on 20 December.

claims.text: Gomułka faced down Khrushchev in October 1956.
claims.note: Khrushchev arrived with top Soviet generals on 19 October; after tense talks he backed off, and Gomułka was elected party leader on 21 October.

claims.text: West German Chancellor Willy Brandt fell to his knees at the Warsaw Ghetto memorial.
claims.note: It happened on 7 December 1970, the day the treaty was signed. The photos went round the world.

claims.text: "Janek Wiśniewski", the young man carried dead on a door in Gdynia, was a real victim with that name.
claims.note: The name came from a protest song. The victim in the famous scene was 18-year-old Zbigniew Godlewski.

reigns.hook: The new boss is an old miner who grew up in France and Belgium. He goes to the angry shipyards in person, and asks the workers a question.

reigns.tagline: Borrowed billions, a tiny Fiat and a Polish pope
reigns.previously: Troops fire on striking shipyard workers. Gomułka is forced out.
paragraphs: Edward Gierek grew up among Polish miners in France and went down the pit at 13. He fought in the Belgian resistance, came home in 1948 and ran Silesia like a showcase. In January 1971 he went to the Gdańsk shipyard himself and asked the strikers for help. Then he went shopping, with Western loans. New factories, steelworks, flats and motorways went up. From 1973 Poles could buy their own car, the little Fiat 126p, the "Maluch".

It was built on credit. By the late 1970s the debts were huge and the shops were empty again. A price rise in 1976 set off riots in Radom and Ursus, and dissidents set up a committee to help the jailed workers. In 1978 the Archbishop of Kraków, Karol Wojtyła, became Pope John Paul II. In June 1979 he toured Poland and millions came out to hear him. People saw how many of them there were.

In August 1980 the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk went on strike, and the whole coast followed. On 31 August the government signed the Gdańsk Agreement, allowing a free trade union. Solidarity was born. Days later Gierek, ill and blamed for everything, was replaced.

claims.text: Gierek asked "Will you help?" and the shipyard workers shouted back "We will help!"
claims.note: He did ask, but the famous answering chant is doubted; some participants said the crowd's reply was patchy and the TV version was tidied up.

claims.text: John Paul II prayed in Warsaw for the Spirit to "renew the face of the earth. Of this land."
claims.note: He said it in Victory Square on 2 June 1979. Many later saw it as the spark for Solidarity.

reigns.hook: Gierek is gone. The party turns to the man who has watched the police, the army and the Church for it, Stanisław Kania, who must somehow live with a free union.

reigns.tagline: The party boss caught between Solidarity and Moscow
reigns.reignEnded: Voted out by the Central Committee
reigns.previously: Strikes win a free union, Solidarity. Gierek falls.
paragraphs: Stanisław Kania was a farmer's son from a village near Krosno who rose through the party machine. By 1980 he was the Central Committee secretary who watched over the police, the army and the Church. When the August strikes broke Gierek, the party made him First Secretary on 6 September 1980. His job was close to impossible: live with a free trade union, and keep Moscow from losing patience.

Solidarity grew to about ten million members. The courts registered it in November 1980 after a tense standoff. In December Soviet forces massed near the border, and Kania went to a Warsaw Pact summit in Moscow to insist that Poles would sort out their own crisis. In March 1981 police beat up Solidarity activists in Bydgoszcz, and the country came to the brink of a general strike before a last-minute deal.

Moscow kept up the pressure with stern letters, phone calls from Brezhnev and military exercises. In July 1981 a party congress re-elected Kania in a secret ballot. But the shops were empty, Solidarity's congress in Gdańsk sent greetings to workers across the Soviet bloc, and Kania still would not use force. On 18 October 1981 the Central Committee voted him out.

claims.text: The Soviet Union was ready to invade Poland in December 1980.
claims.note: Warsaw Pact troops were massed and US intelligence feared an invasion. Kania credited his plea at the 5 December Moscow summit; Soviet papers suggest the Kremlin was reluctant to go in.

claims.text: Solidarity's congress sent a message of support to workers across Eastern Europe.
claims.note: The 'Message to the Working People of Eastern Europe' was adopted on 8 September 1981. Moscow called it a provocation.

claims.text: Kania was later put on trial over martial law and acquitted.
claims.note: Prosecutors charged him alongside Jaruzelski and others in 2007. A Warsaw court acquitted him in 2012.

reigns.hook: Ten million Poles are in Solidarity and Moscow has run out of patience with Kania. The man it now trusts to restore order is a general in dark glasses.

reigns.tagline: The general who sent in the tanks, then gave in
reigns.reignEnded: Handed over to an elected president
reigns.previously: Kania won't crush Solidarity. Moscow wants a tougher man.
paragraphs: Stanisław Kania ran the party for a year after Gierek. Then the job went to Wojciech Jaruzelski, a stiff general from a gentry family. In 1941 the Soviets had deported his family to Siberia, where his father died. He came back with the Polish army formed in the USSR. He was already defence minister and prime minister. In October 1981 he took the party too.

Early on 13 December 1981 he declared martial law on television. Tanks filled the streets, phones went dead and thousands of Solidarity activists, Wałęsa among them, were interned. At the Wujek mine, police shot nine miners dead. Solidarity was banned. In 1984 secret police officers kidnapped and murdered Father Jerzy Popiełuszko, a priest whose sermons drew huge crowds.

By 1988 the economy was in ruins and strikes were back. In 1989 Jaruzelski's team sat down with Solidarity at the Round Table. In the partly free elections of 4 June, Solidarity won almost every seat it was allowed to contest. Jaruzelski became president by one vote, and Tadeusz Mazowiecki became the first non-communist prime minister in the Soviet bloc. Then he agreed to step down early.

claims.text: He wore dark glasses because Siberian snow damaged his eyes.
claims.note: Jaruzelski said so throughout his life, and biographers accept it: snow-blindness while doing forced labour in the Altai in the early 1940s.

claims.text: Martial law saved Poland from a Soviet invasion.
claims.note: Jaruzelski insisted on it until he died. Soviet Politburo papers released later suggest Moscow had already decided not to send troops.

claims.text: Father Popiełuszko was murdered by officers of the communist secret police.
claims.note: Four officers were tried and convicted at Toruń in 1985. Who gave the order has never been settled.

reigns.hook: Communism is gone, but the general is still president. Poles want to choose their own, and the shipyard electrician wants the job.

paragraphs: From here the deck follows the presidents. Lech Wałęsa was an electrician at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk, fired in 1976 for union activity. In August 1980 he joined the strike and soon led it, signing the Gdańsk Agreement with a giant souvenir pen. Under martial law he was interned for nearly a year. In 1983 he won the Nobel Peace Prize, and his wife Danuta collected it in Oslo for him.

He led Solidarity's side at the 1989 Round Table and in 1990 ran for president, beating the outsider Stan Tymiński in the run-off. At his inauguration the last president-in-exile, Ryszard Kaczorowski, handed him the pre-war state insignia. These were the years of "shock therapy", Leszek Balcerowicz's crash switch to a market economy: prices freed, inflation tamed, but many jobs lost.
The last Russian combat troops left in 1993. Wałęsa clashed constantly with parliament and governments. In 1995 he lost a close run-off to the ex-communist Aleksander Kwaśniewski.

claims.text: Wałęsa got into the shipyard to join the strike by climbing over the fence.
claims.note: That is his own account of 14 August 1980, and the jump became the founding image of Solidarity.

claims.text: Danuta Wałęsa collected the Nobel Peace Prize for him.
claims.note: He stayed in Poland in December 1983, fearing he would not be allowed back in. She accepted it with their son Bogdan.

claims.text: The last president-in-exile handed Wałęsa the insignia of the pre-war republic.
claims.note: Ryszard Kaczorowski brought them from London to his swearing-in in December 1990, ending the government-in-exile.

reigns.hook: The man who beats the legend is a smooth, young ex-communist minister who is very good on television.

reigns.tagline: The ex-communist who took Poland into NATO and the EU
reigns.previously: Wałęsa, the Solidarity legend, loses the 1995 vote.
paragraphs: Aleksander Kwaśniewski had been a young sports minister in the last communist governments and sat at the Round Table on the government side. Afterwards he rebuilt the old party into a modern centre-left one. In 1995 he beat Wałęsa by a few points, and many old Solidarity voters were horrified.

He turned out to be a calm, popular president. A new constitution was passed in 1997 and approved in a referendum. In 1999 Poland joined NATO, and on 1 May 2004 it joined the European Union. In 2000 he was re-elected in the first round. He sent Polish troops into the 2003 invasion of Iraq, and in 2004 he helped broker talks in Ukraine's Orange Revolution. After two full terms he had to stand down.

claims.note: He took about 54 percent in the first round; Wałęsa, trying for a comeback, got about 1 percent.

claims.text: Polish special forces took part in the 2003 invasion of Iraq.
claims.note: GROM commandos fought alongside US and British forces; Poland then led a multinational division in Iraq.

claims.text: The 1997 constitution was approved by referendum.
claims.note: Voters backed it on 25 May 1997, though turnout was only about 43 percent.

paragraphs: Lech Kaczyński and his identical twin Jarosław were famous at 12, starring in the 1962 children's film "The Two Who Stole the Moon". Lech became a labour lawyer, advised the Gdańsk strikers in 1980 and was interned under martial law. With his brother he founded the Law and Justice party (PiS). As Mayor of Warsaw he opened the Warsaw Rising Museum in 2004.

In 2005 he beat Donald Tusk for the presidency. For a while in 2006 and 2007 his twin was prime minister. Lech was a firm conservative and deeply wary of Russia. In August 2008 he flew to Tbilisi during Russia's war with Georgia and warned that Ukraine, the Baltic states and Poland could be next.

On 10 April 2010 he flew to Russia for a ceremony marking 70 years since the Katyn massacre. His plane crashed while trying to land in thick fog near Smolensk. All 96 people aboard died, including his wife Maria, the army chief of staff and the last president-in-exile. The cause became a bitter political dispute in Poland.

claims.text: The Kaczyński twins starred together in a children's film.
claims.note: They played the two boys in "O dwóch takich, co ukradli księżyc" (1962), based on a book by Kornel Makuszyński.

claims.text: In Tbilisi he warned that after Georgia, Russia could turn on Ukraine, the Baltics and Poland.
claims.note: He said it at a rally in Tbilisi on 12 August 2008, alongside the leaders of Ukraine and the Baltic states.

claims.text: The Polish government's 2011 investigation blamed a descent below safe height in fog.
claims.note: The state accident commission's report also criticised the Russian air traffic controllers. Later inquiries reached different conclusions and remain disputed.

reigns.hook: Under the constitution, the Speaker of the Sejm takes over that same day. His name is Bronisław Komorowski, and an early election must follow.

paragraphs: Bronisław Komorowski was a historian and an old opposition activist, interned under martial law, who had been defence minister and then Speaker of the Sejm. When the president's plane went down on 10 April 2010, the constitution made him acting head of state the same day.

In the early election that summer he ran for Civic Platform, the party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk, and beat the dead president's twin, Jarosław Kaczyński, in the run-off. He was sworn in on 6 August 2010. His were quiet years at the top: steady growth, and Poland co-hosting the Euro 2012 football championship with Ukraine. In 2015 he looked a safe bet for a second term, then lost the run-off to Andrzej Duda.

reigns.tagline: Ten years of court fights and a war next door
reigns.previously: Komorowski, once the clear favourite, loses the 2015 race.
paragraphs: Andrzej Duda was a lawyer from Kraków who had worked in Lech Kaczyński's chancellery and sat briefly in the European Parliament. Running for Law and Justice (PiS), he won the 2015 run-off with 51.55 percent. That autumn PiS won a majority in parliament on its own, and set about remaking the courts and the constitutional tribunal. Brussels accused Poland of undermining the rule of law, and in 2017 it launched the EU's Article 7 procedure.

Duda mostly signed what the government sent him, though in July 2017, after mass street protests, he vetoed two of its court laws. He won a second term in 2020, narrowly beating Rafał Trzaskowski. When Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, millions of refugees crossed into Poland, and Poles opened their homes to them. In 2023 PiS lost power to Tusk's coalition, and Duda's last years were a running feud with the new government.

claims.text: Duda vetoed two of the government's court reforms in 2017.
claims.note: He announced the vetoes on 24 July 2017 after protests across Poland; he signed revised versions later that year.

claims.text: The EU triggered Article 7 against Poland over the rule of law.
claims.note: The European Commission started the procedure in December 2017, the first time it had ever been used.

claims.text: Duda won the 2020 run-off by about two points.

paragraphs: Karol Nawrocki grew up in Gdańsk, boxed and played football as a young man, and became a historian of the anti-communist resistance. He ran the Museum of the Second World War in Gdańsk from 2017, then the Institute of National Remembrance, which keeps the communist secret police files. PiS picked him in late 2024, though he ran as an independent "citizens' candidate".

He came second in the first round, then beat Warsaw's mayor Rafał Trzaskowski in the run-off on 1 June 2025 with 50.89 percent. He was sworn in on 6 August 2025. He quickly picked fights with Tusk's government, vetoing its bills and sending in his own. He demanded war reparations from Germany, called for a new constitution, and in June 2026 stripped Ukraine's President Zelensky of Poland's highest honour. His story is still being written.

claims.text: Nawrocki won the presidency by under two points.
claims.note: Official results gave him 50.89 percent to Trzaskowski's 49.11 in the run-off of 1 June 2025.

claims.text: He wrote a crime book under a pen name, then praised it as if it were someone else's.
claims.note: He published a book about a communist-era gangster as "Tadeusz Batyr" and admitted it after journalists exposed it during the 2025 campaign.

claims.text: He revoked Zelensky's Order of the White Eagle.
